name: Minutemen
label: SST
lede: Three friends from San Pedro wrote songs that ended before a DJ could find the volume knob, then fit 45 of them on one record. A year and a half later a van axle broke on Interstate 10 and the band was over.

hero.by: Mike Watt, D. Boon and George Hurley, 1982. Wikimedia Commons

eras.title: A boy falls out of a tree
eras.text: D. Boon and Mike Watt were San Pedro harbor-town kids with pawnshop guitars and a habit of copying records. After the Reactionaries fizzled they started over with no frontman and no wasted seconds, and Black Flag gave them their first record.

yt: We Jam Econo: The Story of the Minutemen (2005 documentary)
years.h: D. Boon and Mike Watt start the Reactionaries in San Pedro
years.p: With drummer [[George Hurley|e3644b83-1c19-41fa-bf81-483551cd1588]] and singer Martin Tamburovich, they rehearse a lot and play out rarely. The frontman is the part Boon and Watt later throw out as bourgeois.
years.xp:
Watt was 13 and walking through a San Pedro park when Boon, playing army with other boys, fell out of a tree right next to him. Watt's mother encouraged both boys to learn instruments, and Boon's mother taught him guitar. Watt took bass.

Their first instruments came from a pawnshop, one for $15 and one for $13. Boon's father was a navy veteran who installed radios in Buicks, and the family lived in converted World War II barracks used as public housing. Boon grew up on Buck Owens and Creedence Clearwater Revival; Watt brought him Blue Öyster Cult and the Who.

years.h: A welder named Frank Tonche drums at the first Minutemen gigs
years.p: D. Boon and Mike Watt write their first songs and play a couple of gigs with Tonche. The name is part colonial militia, part dig at a 1960s right-wing group, part 'minute' as in small.
years.xp:
Watt's own account: the name came "partly from the fabled minutemen militia of colonial times and partly to lampoon a right-wing reactionary group of the 1960s."

The band had gone a month without a drummer before the welder sat down.

years.h: The first show is an opening slot for Black Flag, at home
years.p: Minutemen open for [[Black Flag|9941a936-196a-4a62-ae53-a69cbc33f20e]] in San Pedro. [[Greg Ginn|4f35de64-27ab-4426-95fd-8d454cda4e48]] likes what he hears and offers a record on his new label, SST.

years.h: George Hurley takes the drum stool for good
years.p: Frank Tonche leaves, saying he doesn't like the crowd the band is drawing. Hurley, who drummed in the Reactionaries, is back.

years.h: Paranoid Time runs seven songs in 6 minutes 31 seconds
years.p: Greg Ginn produces. The session at Media Art in Hermosa Beach on July 20 is nearly all live, with no overdubs except backing vocals, and [[Raymond Pettibon|3e603b97-d5f8-4547-891b-74cdfd2ed7bf]] draws the cover.
years.xp:
Mike Watt can be heard directing his bandmates before 'Joe McCarthy's Ghost', and George Hurley's brother Greg sings backup. Early covers were printed black, later ones green.

Trouser Press called it "dogmatic politics redeemed by idiosyncratic Wire-type songs." AllMusic's Stephen Thomas Erlewine heard "a startlingly coherent set of primal minimalism."

Ginn walked Watt and Boon through how a record gets made, and they took notes: next came their own label, New Alliance.

eras.title: Jamming econo
eras.text: Minutemen worked like the dockworkers around them: sessions after midnight at cut rates, songs under a minute, vans instead of hotels. Watt called it jamming econo, and it became a creed for American indie rock.

years.h: Watt and Boon start a label of their own with the Joy EP
years.p: Joy is New Alliance No. 3, with cover art by D. Boon. Mike Watt had learned the ropes from Greg Ginn at SST.

years.h: The Punch Line crams 18 songs onto the first album
years.p: SST 004 runs about a quarter hour: D. Boon's scratchy guitar, Mike Watt's lead bass and George Hurley's drums, mostly without a verse-chorus structure in sight. Boon drew the cover.

years.cap: Minutemen in front of a wall of punk flyers, 1982
years.src: Wikipedia: Minutemen discography · Past Daily: Minutemen live at KPFK, 1982
years.h: A Bean-Spill EP and a night on KPFK
years.p: Minutemen put out the Bean-Spill EP on Thermidor and play a live set on Los Angeles community station KPFK on November 27, 1982.
years.xp:
KPFK is a Pacifica station. Past Daily posted the broadcast in 2019, with Dave Alvin of the Blasters on the band: "one of the finest combos to step on to a beer-soaked stage."

Past Daily hears the set as a picture of what the band would be up to in 1983.

years.h: The second album, What Makes a Man Start Fires?, lets funk and jazz in
years.p: SST 014 comes out in January 1983, 14 months after The Punch Line, with the hardcore speed intact.

years.src: Wikipedia: Minutemen discography · Wikipedia: Double Nickels on the Dime
years.h: Buzz or Howl goes out while the band is already recording Double Nickels
years.p: Buzz or Howl Under the Influence of Heat, SST 016, comes out in the same month Minutemen start work on the double album with Ethan James at Radio Tokyo.

eras.title: Forty-five songs at 55 miles an hour
eras.text: Hüsker Dü made a double album, so Minutemen made one with more songs, for $1,100. Eighteen months later they were opening for R.E.M. with a commercial sound and talking about a triple album. Then Boon was gone.

years.big: They gave us the idea to make a double album.
q: It wasn't really a competition even.
years.src: Wikipedia: Double Nickels on the Dime
years.h: Hüsker Dü's Zen Arcade sends Minutemen back to write a double
years.p: Labelmates [[Hüsker Dü|5c4c90a4-539f-4101-83cf-301bc6a94e06]] put out the double Zen Arcade first. Mike Watt, D. Boon and George Hurley write enough songs for a double of their own.
years.xp: Watt wrote 'Take that Hüskers!' on the record, but says it was a thank-you. Each member picked the songs for a side, a plan borrowed from Pink Floyd's Ummagumma, and the fourth side, the leftovers, is labeled 'Side Chaff'.

years.cap: Mike Watt's Volkswagen Beetle at 55 mph on Interstate 10, headed for San Pedro
years.src: Wikipedia: Double Nickels on the Dime · Wikipedia: Minutemen (band)
years.h: Watt drives 55 on Interstate 10 for the Double Nickels on the Dime cover
years.p: The album is 45 songs over four sides, cut at Radio Tokyo in Venice with producer Ethan James and mixed in one night on an eight-track, for $1,100.
years.xp:
Dirk Vandenberg shot the cover from the back seat as Watt drove his Volkswagen Beetle at exactly 55 on Interstate 10 toward San Pedro. It took three loops and two days, and a printing error cut the word 'Pedro' off the sign. The idea owes something to Kraftwerk's Autobahn.

The title answers Sammy Hagar's 'I Can't Drive 55'. Watt: "the big rebellion thing was writing your own fuckin' songs."

'History Lesson - Part II', 'Corona' and 'Jesus and Tequila' are here, plus covers of Creedence Clearwater Revival's 'Don't Look Now', Van Halen's 'Ain't Talkin' 'bout Love' and Steely Dan's 'Dr. Wu'.

Spin gave it 10 out of 10 and Pitchfork put it at No. 17 of the 1980s. It sold 15,000 copies in 1984 and is still the band's best seller. Watt later called it "the best album I ever played on."

years.src: Wikipedia: Double Nickels on the Dime · Wikipedia: Minutemen (band)
years.h: 'History Lesson – Part II' tells the band's own story
years.p: On Double Nickels on the Dime, D. Boon and Mike Watt trace how they got from San Pedro to a record. Michael Azerrad would take the title of his 2001 book, Our Band Could Be Your Life, from a line in it.

yt: Full live set at The Stone, San Francisco, May 13, 1985
years.h: Project: Mersh goes for radio and the underground says no
years.p: Six songs aimed at radio; the title is San Pedro slang for commercial. The reaction from inside the underground is bad, and it sells poorly next to Double Nickels on the Dime.
years.xp:
It is the band's most commercial-sounding record, and Wikipedia ties its weak sales largely to that negative reaction from the underground.

The clip is a full set from The Stone in San Francisco on May 13, 1985, the month before the EP came out.

years.h: Minutemen and Black Flag record Minuteflag together
years.p: The two SST bands cut a joint EP in 1985, and the label holds it until early 1986, after D. Boon's death.

years.h: Charlotte, North Carolina, opening for R.E.M.: the last Minutemen show
years.p: It closes a tour with [[R.E.M.|ea4dfa26-f633-4da6-a52a-f49ea4897b58]] and comes nine days before D. Boon's death.

years.h: The last album, 3-Way Tie (For Last), is out the month the band ends
years.p: SST 058 comes out in December 1985, with cover art drawn by D. Boon.

years.big: A rock death that for wasted potential has Lennon and Hendrix for company.
years.h: D. Boon dies in a van crash on Interstate 10 in Arizona
years.p: Around 4:40 a.m., east of Quartzsite, the van's rear axle breaks. D. Boon, lying in the back with a fever and no seatbelt, is thrown out and dies of a broken neck at 27. The quote is critic Robert Christgau's.
years.xp:
His girlfriend Linda Kite was driving. D. Boon had been born in San Pedro on April 1, 1958.

Watt has said he and Boon had just been talking about a triple album. Minutemen ended that morning; Watt and Hurley refused to go on under the name.

Watt has dedicated every album since to Boon's memory, and Rolling Stone ranks him No. 89 among the greatest guitarists.

eras.title: Sonic Youth hands Watt a bass
eras.text: Watt fell into a deep depression, and he and Hurley meant to quit music altogether. Friends in New York and a fan from Ohio talked them back into it.

q: Thurston asked me to play bass on Evol. That was a big highlight, man.
years.h: Thurston Moore asks Mike Watt to play bass on EVOL
years.p: Watt goes to New York and plays on [[Sonic Youth|5cbef01b-cc35-4f52-af7b-d0df0c4f61b9]]'s EVOL. The Ciccone Youth side project is dreamed up partly to get him making music again.

years.h: A fan from Ohio talks Watt and Hurley into fIREHOSE
years.p: Ohio State student [[Ed Crawford|c02f03fe-93cf-4590-841b-1b9f04d6a694]] talks his way into a jam with Mike Watt and George Hurley. The lowercase f nods to the all-caps Minutemen logo.
years.xp: fIREHOSE went on to sign with Columbia Records and broke up in 1993.

years.h: Ballot Result lets the fans pick the live record
years.p: SST 068: Mike Watt and George Hurley mail out ballots and build a live double album from the votes, with recordings from September 1980 to November 30, 1985.

eras.title: Our band could be your life
eras.text: Years after the crash, Minutemen found a bigger audience than they ever had: a stunt show's theme, a book named for one of their songs, and a documentary that premiered in the town that made them.

years.h: 'Corona' becomes the Jackass theme
years.p: The instrumental parts of D. Boon's 'Corona', from Double Nickels on the Dime, open MTV's stunt show, which puts Minutemen on MTV.

years.h: Azerrad's Our Band Could Be Your Life gives them a chapter
years.p: Michael Azerrad's history of 1980s American indie rock takes its title from a Minutemen song. His argument is that they proved regular Joes could make great art.

years.cap: Mike Watt on bass at the Khyber, Philadelphia, October 29, 2004
years.h: Watt and Hurley play Minutemen songs as a duo, bass and drums only
years.p: On rare nights, mostly around Los Angeles, they play a set of Minutemen songs. No one fills in for D. Boon, and they won't bill it as Minutemen.

years.h: We Jam Econo premieres in San Pedro, at the Warner Grand
years.p: Tim Irwin's documentary We Jam Econo: The Story of the Minutemen premieres in the band's hometown theater in February 2005. The DVD follows in June 2006.
